title: Attend
text:
03-06 Dec 2026 / TBarM Resort, New Braunfels TX
The workshop is capped at roughly 60 people: working trainers, tactical practitioners, and training-science researchers. If you train law enforcement or tactical professionals, or study how that training works, this room is for you.

title: Attend
text:
What it costs
Attending costs $695, which covers your room and board at TBarM Resort for three nights (December 3, 4, and 5) plus all meals from dinner on December 3 through breakfast on December 6. Travel to and from New Braunfels is on you.
Selected presenters attend at no cost: conference fee waived, room and board covered, and travel arranged and paid by the workshop. One presenter per session is covered; co-presenters are welcome at their own cost.

title: Attend
text:
How to register
To register, email Sarah E. Drennan at sd33@txstate.edu with your name, agency or affiliation, and contact information.

Seats are limited and the room fills with a mix of roles on purpose, so register early. Most of the 2026 seats are already spoken for.

title: Attend
text:
The venue
TBarM Resort sits on the Guadalupe River in New Braunfels, Texas, between San Antonio and Austin in the Hill Country. Sessions, meals, and lodging are all on site, which is part of the design: the conversations that start on the mat keep going at dinner.
A few practical notes:

No live-fire range. Demonstrations use sims, scenarios, and mat work.
Airports. San Antonio International (SAT) and Austin-Bergstrom (AUS) are both within about an hour’s drive. Rental car or rideshare from either works.
Weather. Early December in the Hill Country is usually mild, roughly 40s to 60s Fahrenheit, but pack a layer for cool mornings.

title: Attend
text:
The rhythm of the week
Arrive Thursday December 3 in time for dinner. Friday and Saturday are full session days, everyone in the same room. Sunday morning is breakfast, an informal wrap-up, and checkout. See the schedule for the day-by-day outline.

title: About
text:
The Advanced Training Design Workshop is a small, annual working conference for people who train law enforcement and tactical professionals. Roughly 60 people attend: working trainers, tactical practitioners, and training-science researchers, all in one room for two full days of hands-on sessions. The 2026 theme is Designing Training That Transfers.
The workshop grew out of the ALERRT Center’s ongoing ecological dynamics seminar series, which brings training-science researchers and practitioners together around how people actually learn, perceive, and decide under pressure. The workshop keeps that spirit but widens the door: no particular theoretical school is required. Presenters show their method live, explain why they do it that way, and the room takes it from there.

title: Call for Presentations
text:
What we look for
Any aspect of law enforcement or tactical training methodology: scenario design, decision-making under stress, integrated response, use of force, debrief and feedback, fitness and readiness, skill transfer, instructor development, or anything else interesting you are doing. No particular theoretical school is required. What matters is that you can show the method and explain why you do it that way.
Slots are limited, and selection is worth the effort: selected presenters have their conference fee, room, board, and travel covered.

title: Call for Presentations
text:
The session format
Every session is 50 minutes, in front of the whole room:

Hands-on demonstration (~25 min). Run your method live. Attendees participate or observe up close.
What and why (~15 min). Explain the method, the reasoning behind it, and the evidence or experience it rests on.
Audience input and Q&A (~10 min). The room pushes back, asks questions, and offers alternatives.

TBarM has no live-fire range. Sims, scenarios, and mat work are all fine.

title: Call for Presentations
text:
What a proposal includes
Proposals are a single Word or PDF document with:

Session title
Lead presenter: name, agency or affiliation, email, phone, and a 100-word bio
Co-presenter(s), if any, with the same fields
Abstract (400 words or fewer): what you will demonstrate, what you will explain, and what attendees take away
Demonstration plan (300 words or fewer): what the demo looks like, the active vs. observer split, equipment and space needs, and safety
Rationale (300 words or fewer): why this method, plus your experience, evidence, and the trade-offs
Logistical needs, itemized: equipment, props, AV, space, and setup time
Prior delivery: have you taught this before, and where?

title: The Advanced TrainingDesign Workshop 2026
text:
Not a lecture hall
The audience is a mix of working trainers, tactical practitioners, and training-science researchers. The point of the room is not to sit through talks. It is to put methods on the mat, in front of people who train for a living, and take them apart together.


Watch
Every session opens with a hands-on demonstration. Presenters run their method live, with attendees on the mat or close enough to see the details.


Ask
Hard questions are the point. Presenters explain what they do and why, then the room pushes on the evidence, the trade-offs, and the edge cases.


Take home
The goal for every attendee is the same: leave with something you can use in your next training cycle.

title: Empowering Feedback: Enhancing Student Learning Through Socratic Feedback
text: Friday 04 Dec / 9:00 AM / Raptor Public Safety Coaching

title: Empowering Feedback: Enhancing Student Learning Through Socratic Feedback
text:
The session
A classroom session on feedback: the types available to a coach, what each type does to student motivation and focus of attention, how to avoid building students who depend on the coach for every answer, and the use of video as a feedback tool. Attendees pair up and practice Socratic feedback, first on everyday problems and then on common law enforcement problems.

title: Empowering Feedback: Enhancing Student Learning Through Socratic Feedback
text:

title: Micro Doses = Massive Impact: Roll Call Training for Patrol Excellence
text: Friday 04 Dec / 4:00 PM / Chief of Police, Town of Colonie, New York

title: Micro Doses = Massive Impact: Roll Call Training for Patrol Excellence
text:
The session
In September 2025, the Colonie Police Department replaced conventional roll call with a 13-week micro-dosing program: 15-to-20-minute training modules delivered inside daily patrol briefings. Chief Gerace runs the room through a live micro-dose exactly as delivered at roll call, including a rapid tactical decision game with volunteers in the hot seat. He then presents the Finn Institute’s evaluation findings: measured gains in knowledge retention, movement from needs-improvement to mastery in life-saving procedures, and increased decision-making confidence among less-experienced officers. Attendees leave with the program schedule and implementation suggestions.

An FBI National Academy graduate, he holds a gubernatorial appointment to the New York State Municipal Police Training Council and has spoken before the National Academy of Sciences on behavioral health emergencies and modern restraint. His work appears in the FBI Law Enforcement Bulletin, Police Chief Magazine, Police1, and Translational Criminology.

title: The Tri-Axial Scaffolding Framework for Task Learning
text: Friday 04 Dec / 3:00 PM / Jefferson Parish Sheriff’s Office / Clemson University

title: The Tri-Axial Scaffolding Framework for Task Learning
text:
The session
Scaffolding, any assistance that lets a student perform beyond current unassisted capability, is among the best-supported concepts in the learning sciences. The open question is where to put it. The tri-axial framework specifies whether a scaffold should be located, faded, or embedded based on learner expertise, task complexity, and environmental dependence. Three demonstrations run in one session (a threshold evaluation, hand control on the mats, and a criminal statute in the classroom) with the presenters explaining what is being scaffolded, how, and why as each unfolds.
Co-presenting with David Dalton and David Short.

He has an extensive combat sports coaching background with athletes successful at national and international level.

title: You’ve Got To Be Joking! A Humor Workshop for Trainers

The session
Before students can retain anything, the trainer has to win their attention, and humor is a reliable way to get it. This classroom session covers why humor makes training engaging and memorable, basic joke structure and joke-writing technique, and how to add humor to a slide deck with images. Participants run improv exercises to build the mindset, then write and immediately deliver their own material.

title: Scenario First: Training Adaptable Responders for Uncertain Environments
text: Saturday 05 Dec / 1:00 PM / Abbotsford Police Department / Wolf Training Systems

title: Scenario First: Training Adaptable Responders for Uncertain Environments
text:
The session
Massive hemorrhage control is the working example; scenario design is the subject. Two officers respond to a shots-fired scene with an officer down and bleeding out. Rather than teaching every intervention first, the session starts with the problem and shapes performance with short pauses, focused teaching, Socratic questioning, and immediate rewinds. Complexity builds one layer at a time, from extremity bleeding through tourniquet transition, junctional bleeding, wound packing, and neck bleeding, while the learner stays inside a meaningful tactical problem. Attendees leave with a repeatable structure that transfers to use of force, de-escalation, arrest and control, vehicle stops, and room clearing.

He is founder of Wolf Training Systems and Chief Operating Officer and Lead Instructor for the Joint Tactical Medical Program, which delivers tactical medical training to agencies across Canada.

title: Prone Restraint Through a Constraints-Led Approach
text: Friday 04 Dec / 11:00 AM / Winnebago County Sheriff’s Office, Rockford, Illinois

title: Prone Restraint Through a Constraints-Led Approach
text:
The session
A mat session that teaches prone control as constraint manipulation rather than memorized technique, built on three control intentions: maximizing the subject’s body-to-ground contact, separating the knees and elbows to deny a base, and clear officer-to-officer communication. Instruction begins at the end state, a subject already controlled prone, and works backward through representative tasks at varying levels of resistance, team configuration, and environment.

title: Prone Restraint Through a Constraints-Led Approach
text:
About the presenter
Bryce has served with the Winnebago County Sheriff’s Office for over 27 years and has supervised the Training Division for 12. He holds instructor certifications in firearms, defensive tactics, less-lethal weapons, active shooter response, de-escalation, and tactical medicine, has authored several state-certified curricula, and is a former world-ranked professional fighter.

title: Training the Decision, Not Just the Skill: Improving Threat Recognition and Response
text: Saturday 05 Dec / 8:00 AM / Lieutenant, Cobb County Police Department, Marietta, Georgia

title: Training the Decision, Not Just the Skill: Improving Threat Recognition and Response
text:
The session
Pre-assault indicators are usually taught in a classroom as isolated cues, and weapon presentation is trained statically off an audible stimulus, so officers never learn to couple the two. Using blank-firing simulation pistols, this session trains threat perception and firearm access together, treating suspect movement as actionable rather than descriptive. The approach draws on Left of Bang and recognition-primed decision making, and scaffolds out to cover, team movement, and crossfire considerations.

title: Training the Decision, Not Just the Skill: Improving Threat Recognition and Response

Giesler has served with Cobb County PD since 2007 across patrol, the violent street crimes unit, and a narcotics task force, and served as Range Master at the county Public Safety Training Center. He reviews departmental use of force incidents and teaches use of force to all recruits. He is a Force Science Advanced Specialist, a Georgia POST use of force and defensive tactics instructor, and a Master PepperBall Instructor.

title: Beyond the Tug-of-War: Grappling-Based Methods for Safe Hand Extraction During Prone Resistance
text: Friday 04 Dec / 2:00 PM / Austin Police Department

title: Beyond the Tug-of-War: Grappling-Based Methods for Safe Hand Extraction During Prone Resistance
text:
The session
A mat session, mostly demonstration, on the prone subject who tucks his hands under his torso and will not give them up. It opens by recreating the scenario and showing why direct pulling fails and how some officer actions strengthen the subject’s defensive structure. It then works positional dominance, leverage, and structural manipulation to weaken resistance before attempting extraction, reducing the need to escalate with strikes or tools.
Co-presenting with Adam Kaufman (Austin Police Department), a Senior Police Officer, FTO, Mental Health Officer, and Special Response Team member who supports Austin Police Jiu-Jitsu through curriculum development and program evaluation, and previously worked with the National Policing Institute.

title: Beyond the Tug-of-War: Grappling-Based Methods for Safe Hand Extraction During Prone Resistance

The session works from a basic Axon TASER scenario that most attendees will already know and shows how Denver scales it for learners at different experience levels: bringing the drill to life, manipulating constraints, and applying the feedback models the department uses with both trainers and trainees.

title: When They Bring a Knife to a Gunfight: Training for Real-World Weapon Encounters
text: Saturday 05 Dec / 10:00 AM / Head Coach, SBG Athens

title: When They Bring a Knife to a Gunfight: Training for Real-World Weapon Encounters
text:
The session
Most counter-edged-weapon systems teach scripted slash-and-block sequences and choreographed disarms that collapse under live pressure. This mat session, with the whole room working in pairs, integrates weapon management into existing standing grappling and hand-fighting frameworks instead of isolating it. A live, unscripted knife enters the clinch, and the defender manages control, weapon suppression, and the transition to cuffing at once, under a strict safety commitment. Attendees leave with a scalable framework for introducing live decision-making and variable complexity into an agency defensive tactics program.

title: When They Bring a Knife to a Gunfight: Training for Real-World Weapon Encounters

He is co-author of “Applying an ecological dynamics framework to mixed martial arts training.”

title: Constraints-Led Instruction for Room Entry and Hallway Movement
text: Friday 04 Dec / 1:00 PM / Boise Police Department

title: Constraints-Led Instruction for Room Entry and Hallway Movement
text:
The session
A constraints-led build of active attacker tactics, run in hallway and room space. Role players wearing colored pennies (suspect, officer, innocent, unknown) stage at varying depths in rooms off a hallway while solo officers work the hall. Early repetitions hold officers close to or far from doorways so they feel distance and angle; the restrictions then come off, and officers self-organize toward the serpentine pattern. Room entries run under spacing constraints rather than scripted assignments. The trade: less explicit instruction, more active engagement per training hour.

title: Constraints-Led Instruction for Room Entry and Hallway Movement
text:

He is the lead Taser instructor, an Idaho Master Instructor for Defensive Tactics, and a BJJ black belt, with prior service as a SWAT operator, FTO, detective, and supervisor across 22 years in law enforcement.

title: From Techniques to Adaptability: An Ecological Approach to Weapons-Based Defensive Tactics
text:
The session
A practical introduction to weapons-based defensive tactics on the mats with training weapons, aimed at developing officers who perceive opportunities and act rather than officers who apply prescribed solutions to predetermined problems. Small-sided games and designed constraints work across the operational ranges: handfighting, clinch and wall-pin, grounded encounters, and the transitions between them. Covers representative learning design, implementation inside an existing defensive tactics program, and the common misconceptions and lessons learned along the way.

title: The Problem-First Approach to Control Tactics Training
text: Friday 04 Dec / 10:00 AM / Walworth County Sheriff’s Office / C4C Police Jiu-Jitsu

title: The Problem-First Approach to Control Tactics Training
text:
The session
A mat session that organizes control tactics training around problem spaces rather than prescribed technique progressions, using the 3Ms model: maintaining control, modifying control, and making control. Participants work in groups of four (two officers, one subject, one safety officer) through three rounds, one per problem space. Each round runs the same cycle: minimum instruction, hands-on exposure with no directed solutions, discussion of what broke down and why, then re-engagement.

title: The Problem-First Approach to Control Tactics Training

About the presenter
Bob is a Wisconsin Certified Law Enforcement Instructor, Corrections Superintendent, Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu black belt, and co-owner of three BJJ academies, with over 20 years in law enforcement and defensive tactics instruction. He has implemented modernized training approaches across multiple agencies and within the Wisconsin statewide curriculum.

title: FAQ
text: Answers to the questions we get most

title: FAQ
text:
Attending

Who is the workshop for?
People who train law enforcement and tactical professionals, and people who study that training. The room is a deliberate mix: working trainers, tactical practitioners, and training-science researchers, about 60 in total. You do not need to be sworn law enforcement to attend.


How much does it cost, and what does that include?
Attending costs $695, which covers your room at TBarM Resort for three nights (December 3, 4, and 5) and all meals from dinner Thursday through breakfast Sunday. Travel is on you. Selected presenters attend at no cost, with travel covered.


How do I register?
Email Sarah E. Drennan at sd33@txstate.edu with your name, agency or affiliation, and contact information. Seats are limited and most of the 2026 room is already spoken for, so register early. Details are on the attend page.


How do I get to TBarM?
TBarM Resort is in New Braunfels, Texas, between San Antonio and Austin. San Antonio International (SAT) and Austin-Bergstrom (AUS) are both within about an hour’s drive; rent a car or use rideshare from either. Everything during the workshop, including sessions, meals, and lodging, is on site, so you will not need a car once you arrive.


What should I bring?
Sessions are hands-on, and most include an active participant role. Bring clothes you can move in. Early December in the Hill Country is usually mild, but pack a layer for cool mornings.


Is there live fire?
No. TBarM has no live-fire range. Demonstrations use sims, scenarios, and mat work.

title: FAQ
text:
Presenting

How do I get a presentation slot?
Through the annual call for presentations, usually posted in the spring with proposals due in early June. The present page has the full requirements and a copy of the most recent call. Selected presenters have their conference fee, room, board, and travel covered.


Can I bring a co-presenter?
Yes. One presenter per session is covered by the workshop; co-presenters are welcome at their own cost.


Do I have to subscribe to a particular training philosophy?
No. No particular theoretical school is required. What matters is that you can show your method live and explain why you do it that way.


What is on the program this year?
Sixteen sessions across Friday and Saturday, opening with a keynote from Rob Gray. The sessions page has a page per session with the full description and the presenter’s bio; the schedule has the running order.

title: FAQ
text:
Materials

Where do slides, white papers, and readings live?
On the resources page. Presenters who want the room to keep their materials email them to sd33@txstate.edu and they get posted there.


Will photos from the workshop be available?
Yes, on the photos page after the workshop. If you have shots from past years, send them in.

title: What lives on this page
text:
As the 2026 workshop comes together, this page will fill with three kinds of material:

White papers and publications that come out of the workshop or the ALERRT Center’s related research.
Session materials: slides, handouts, drill sheets, and scenario templates from presenters who want the room to keep them.
Readings that presenters recommend before or after their sessions.

Everything posted here is meant to be used. Take it back to your agency, adapt it, and tell us how it went.
Presenters: email your materials or links to sd33@txstate.edu and we will post them with your session.
